title: networking-streaming-http-grpc-chunking-overhead-benchmarks
content:
Objective:
Run controlled experiments to quantify networking and streaming overheads in the serving runtime across HTTP (chunked), HTTP/2 gRPC streaming, and with/without common proxies (Envoy). Focus on per-chunk latency, end-to-end generation latency for short and long outputs, CPU/network system overhead, and backpressure/queueing behavior under load.

Summary / TL;DR:
- gRPC streaming (HTTP/2) consistently shows lower per-chunk latency and fewer system call wakeups than HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer for small chunk sizes.
- Small chunk sizes (<=64 tokens) dramatically increase syscall and context-switch overhead; batching chunks into 128–256 token windows gives the best latency/throughput tradeoff.
- Envoy (default config) adds measurable tail latency (~0.8–2.0 ms p95) and can amplify backpressure under high concurrency; bypassing or tuning proxy timeouts reduces this.
- Kernel-level traces (eBPF) show a significant fraction of extra latency spent in sendmsg/epoll wakeups and user-space memcpy for small writes.
- Recommendation: default to HTTP/2 gRPC streaming for low-latency token streaming, implement adaptive chunk sizing on the client (grow chunk if queueing observed), and add a proxy config playbook for low-latency routes.

Test harness / environment:
- Runtime: serving-runtime commit a1b2c3 (profiling branch).
- Hardware: 8x A100-SXM GPUs on an 8-node cluster; each head node: 32 vCPU, 256 GB RAM, 25 Gbps NIC.
- Network: single-region VPC, baseline intra-region p95 RTT 0.45 ms.
- Clients: 50 concurrent connections generating mixed workloads (short gen: 32 tokens target, long gen: 1024 tokens target).
- Workload types: single-stream generation (stream tokens as produced), chunked streaming (batch tokens at client-side chunk sizes: 16, 32, 64, 128, 256), and non-streaming (final response only).
- Protocols tested: HTTP/1.1 chunked transfer, HTTP/2 gRPC streaming, HTTP/1.1 with long-polling (control), TLS enabled in all runs.
- Proxies: direct (no proxy), Envoy (v1.22 default bootstrap), NGINX (basic proxy).
- Measurement tools: wrk/vegeta for load, custom streaming client harness, perf, eBPF/tcptrace, and application-level timing hooks (token emit timestamps).

Benchmarks -- key metrics captured:
- per-chunk latency (ms): time from model token production to chunk bytes being consumed by client read callback
- end-to-end generation latency (ms): request start to final-token-arrival
- system CPU% and NIC utilization sampled during runs
- syscall counts (sendmsg/write, epoll_wait) per second from perf/eBPF
- queuing/backpressure metrics: server queue length, request processing time distributions

Representative results (median/p95 numbers aggregated across nodes):
1) Short generation workload (target 32 tokens):
   - HTTP/1.1 chunked, chunk size 32 tokens: p50 = 18.4 ms, p95 = 42.1 ms, p99 = 78.2 ms
   - gRPC streaming, chunk size 32 tokens: p50 = 15.1 ms, p95 = 27.6 ms, p99 = 48.0 ms
   - HTTP/1.1 chunked, chunk size 16 tokens: p95 increases by ~12–18 ms vs 32-token chunks (higher syscall overhead)
   - Direct vs Envoy: Envoy adds ~0.9 ms p50 and ~1.8 ms p95 in otherwise identical runs (default config).

2) Long generation workload (target 1024 tokens, emitted in chunks):
   - gRPC streaming, chunk size 128 tokens: steady-state token throughput ~6.8 k tokens/s per GPU, p95 per-chunk latency ~35 ms
   - HTTP/1.1 chunked, chunk size 128 tokens: similar throughput but p95 ~45 ms (extra serialization/copying)
   - Larger chunks (256+) reduce per-chunk overhead but increase tail latency for the first tokens (bad for interactive use).

3) Throughput & CPU/network overhead:
   - Small chunks (<=32 tokens) cause 2.5–3x more sendmsg syscalls per second vs 128-token chunks, increasing CPU softirq and context switches by ~30–40%.
   - Observed kernel-level memcpy and send buffer stalls when many small writes are issued back-to-back; NIC throughput remains under link capacity but CPU becomes the bottleneck.

Profiling observations (eBPF / perf):
- sendmsg and writev account for ~12–28% of additional latency on HTTP/1.1 small-chunk runs.
- epoll wakeups scale linearly with number of connections and are amplified by small chunk sizes — fewer, larger writes reduce wakeups.
- In gRPC runs the language runtime (golang) scheduler had fewer runnable procs waiting on network because HTTP/2 multiplexing allows a single connection to amortize TLS and handshake costs.
- Envoy added measurable overhead in two places: (1) buffer copy inside proxy when handling chunked encodings, (2) additional timers/event-loop hops causing tail latency amplification under bursty arrivals.

Proxy-specific notes:
- Envoy default buffer limits and HTTP/1.1 codec path are optimized for throughput, not chatty streaming. Increasing "max_downstream_bytes_per_stream" and tuning "stream_idle_timeout" improved p95 in our tests but introduced risk for memory growth under abuse.
- NGINX showed lower overhead than Envoy in simple passthrough tests but lacks HTTP/2 multiplexing benefits for our test harness (client connections were higher).

Backpressure & queueing behavior:
- When client emission rate > runtime processing rate, we observed queue length growth and higher P99 latencies. Two common failure modes:
  1) Runtime queueing: requests pile up in the token-generation queue; adaptive chunking reduces queue pressure by emitting larger batches less frequently.
  2) Proxy backpressure: Envoy buffers and then signals window updates more slowly, making the client observe stuttering. Reconfiguring window sizes and enabling HTTP/2 flow-control tuning improved behavior.

Recommendations (short):
- Default to HTTP/2 gRPC streaming for interactive streaming endpoints. It gives lower per-chunk latency and fewer syscalls due to multiplexing.
- Implement client-side adaptive chunk sizing: start at 32–64 token chunks; if the client observes steady queueing/tail growth, increase to 128–256 until queueing subsides.
- Add server-side heuristics to merge small token writes within a tight time window (e.g., 2–4 ms) to reduce syscalls without harming perceived interactivity.
- Provide proxy config templates for low-latency streaming (Envoy/Nginx): tune downstream buffer limits, flow-control window sizes, and idle timeouts.
- Add operational dashboards to surface syscall rates (sendmsg/write calls per second), epoll wakeups, and average chunk size to help customers diagnose streaming inefficiency.

Action items / next experiments:
- Run end-to-end tests with real-world client libraries (JS browser, Python async) to validate adaptive chunking UX and confirm perceived latency improvements.
- Profile TLS CPU cost impact for small chunk sizes (measure handshake amortization effects for short-lived connections).
- Evaluate a server-side write coalescer (merge writes within 1–3 ms) and measure p50/p95 improvements under 10–100 concurrent clients.
- Work with platform to publish an "streaming best-practices" doc & Envoy config snippet for enterprise customers.

Appendix: lower-level findings / quick notes:
- Observed packet sizes: very small chunks produce many sub-MTU packets; enabling TCP_CORK-like behavior (coalescing) on server-socket reduced packets and syscalls in lab tests.
- On linux kernels we tested (5.15/6.x), splice/sendfile approaches didn't help (user-space copies still dominate for our framed protobuf payloads).
- For TLS, session reuse and long-lived HTTP/2 connections are critical; avoid connection churn for streaming routes.
